paragraphs: This story comes from an Indian book about the lives of saints. A young Brahmin had fallen for a woman of bad reputation who lived in another village across a wide river. Every day he took the ferry over to see her. One day he had to perform his father's funeral rites. He was desperate to go to her, but the ceremonies could not be skipped, so he sat through them, fuming.

By the time they were over it was night, and a violent storm had blown up. Rain lashed down and the river heaved with huge waves. No ferryman would risk the crossing. But he was mad with longing, so when he spotted a log floating past, he grabbed it, struggled across, tossed it onto the bank and hurried to her house. The doors were shut and no one heard his knocking over the wind. Walking round the walls, he found what seemed to be a rope hanging down. Thinking she had left it for him, he climbed up, slipped on the other side and fell unconscious. The noise brought the woman out.

When he came to, she noticed a terrible smell on him and asked how he had got in. Hadn't she left him a rope? She laughed: did he really think she cared enough for that? They went to look. The 'rope' was a deadly cobra, its head inside a hole; his weight had killed it. The 'log' was a rotting corpse carried down by the flood.

Then she said something that struck him like lightning. Why give your whole heart to someone like me? Give it to God, and you will be perfect. For a moment he glimpsed something beyond. He asked if God was real, and she said yes. He walked into the forest and wept and prayed for years, begging that his enormous love might flow to the infinite.

Later, having become a sannyasin, he saw a beautiful merchant's wife at a river ghat, and the old pull returned; he followed her home. Her husband welcomed the monk and, trusting in God, even introduced his wife. Vilvamangala asked her for two hairpins and drove them into his own eyes, telling them that from now on they would see only Krishna, with the eyes of the soul. Back in the forest he wept and struggled until, the story says, he saw God as Krishna. He wrote beautiful love poems, and as Sanskrit writers salute their Gurus, he saluted that first woman as his first Guru.
learn: Intense passion is not the enemy; its direction is what matters. The energy that drives an obsession can, redirected, drive greatness. And wisdom can come from the least expected person, so stay humble enough to hear it.
